newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: Calls for IMF lifeboat as South African rand sinks.
newsitem.headline: Calls for IMF lifeboat as South African rand sinks.

text.p: There were mounting calls for South Africa to seek International Monetary Fund (IMF) assistance on Wednesday as the rand plunged to new record lows against the dollar and the British pound.

Economists and opposition politicians said Finance Minister Trevor Manuel had little choice but to seek IMF help, despite vociferous opposition from some left-wing members of the ruling African National Congress (ANC).
"Dr Stals (the Reserve Bank governor) and the minister of finance should at least start filling in the forms," said National Party spokesman Theo Alant.
"It is a serious situation and I think they should be looking at the option of an IMF facility. It would send a political signal to the players in the market...that we intend to support the rand."

The battle-scarred currency sank more than five cents to 4.74 against the dollar and to 7.72 against a rampant British pound on Wednesday as speculators sold rands short and importers scrambled to secure cover to pay for essential goods.
It has now lost 30 percent versus the dollar since February.
Intervention by the Reserve Bank failed to stop the slide with currency traders scornful of the country's low reserves.
Economists estimated that foreign reserves, which stood at 10 billion rand ($2.1 billion) at end-September, had probably shrunk by a billion rand on the latest bout of intervention.
"The situation is plain desperate," said Hania Farhan of ING Barings in Johannesburg, urging the government to turn to the IMF.
Under IMF rules, South Africa would be able to draw up to 100 percent of its IMF quota -- or some $2 billion -- for use as a standby or extended fund facility.

Farhan said such a cash injection would boost reserves and reassure the markets that South Africa could fund its current account deficit, thus allowing the lifting of exchange controls on residents which remain a key cause of market uncertainty.

The view was echoed by fund manager BOE Asset Management which said an IMF package was a "sensible" option, especially in view of its belief that the South African budget deficit was much larger than generally acknowledged.
Standard Bank, one of the country's big four lenders, made a similar plea for IMF assistance last week.
Reserve Bank governor Chris Stals has said several times that IMF aid is an option, although the first line of defence to bolster reserves would be overseas credit lines available from foreign banks.
IMF managing director Michel Camdessus said this month that the institution was prepared to support South Africa's reserves and provide funding, if asked.
But many in the ANC are wary of the stigma attached to IMF aid, following unpopular IMF interventions elsewhere in Africa.

"The question of borrowing from the IMF merely to put the money into speculative forces in the market is not the way to go," said ANC member of parliament and deputy chairman of the finance committee, Rob Davies.

Constantin Vayenas, emerging market analyst at UBS in London, said despite domestic opposition, South Africa appeared to be moving closer to an approach to the IMF, although finalising any deal would take several months.

The government's macroeconomic strategy, which won praise from Camdessus during a recent visit, meant there were likely to be minimal extra conditions linked to an IMF loan. However, Vayenas said there could be demands for a firmer commitment on privatisation.
Democratic Party finance spokesman Ken Andrew said the key to stabilising the rand and encouraging fresh investment in South Africa remained the lifting of exchange controls.
"A great deal depends on capital inflows but these will not come in while controls are in place...government should bite the bullet," he said.
Critics say that as long as controls remain it is impossible to determine the correct value of the rand -- although many South Africans are convinced it has fallen too far.

Business Day newspaper said: "There is a sense of bewildered panic as we try to work out why the world hates us so much -- when we thought it would love us for getting rid of apartheid in a relatively peaceful way."
